data.title: Anthropic's post-debut stumble delivers reality check for AI trade
data.description:
Nov 20 (Reuters) - Anthropic's much-hyped arrival on Wall Street fizzled out on Friday as a dramatic unraveling of the AI trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector.

As the first large machine-learning model maker to go public, Anthropic is widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, and its listing had been viewed as a potential boost for a sector struggling to regain its footing.

But the stock was last trading at $87.28, about 10% below Thursday's close and not far from its $83 IPO price, while declines in other technology heavyweights suggested the listing had done little to stem the broader selloff.

"Anthropic faded relatively quickly. I don't think investors believe there's something inherently wrong with the company, management or business. I think they're just skeptical of this market," said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth.

The AI boom has come under pressure over the past month as concerns mount that spending on the technology, expected by some estimates to top $1 trillion this year, is not generating returns quickly enough.

Fears of political hurdles to data center construction and the leadership turmoil at chipmaker Nvidia have also added to those worries.

"Investors still believe in AI but are becoming more selective about what they will pay for that growth," said David Miller, chief investment officer at Catalyst Funds.

Among the Magnificent Seven stocks, Nvidia fell about 6% and Meta Platforms dropped nearly 3%. Amazon and Microsoft lost less than 1% each.

Chip stocks also slid, with AMD and Marvell Technology down over 8% each and Intel losing roughly 3%.

The focus now shifts to a potential listing by another AI leader, OpenAI, which could provide another test of investor appetite for AI stocks. OpenAI has indicated it may go public next year.

Despite a strong IPO pipeline of high-profile AI and infrastructure companies, many have pushed their IPO plans to 2027.

PATIENCE MAY PAY

Anthropic's stock could find support in the coming weeks. London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could account for purchases of up to 30% of Anthropic's shares by year-end.

Near-term volatility, however, could persist as the initial euphoria around the listing fades and investors assess whether a valuation of about 40 times sales over the past 12 months can be sustained.

But Morgan Stanley, the underwriter tasked with stabilizing Anthropic's shares after its market debut, closed a position meant to do that, the company said, removing a potential pillar of support for shares.

Anthropic had a fully diluted valuation of about $1.6 trillion at the latest price, and a market capitalization of $1.2 trillion based on shares outstanding.

"We favor patience on Anthropic and recommend evaluating the company as it reports public results," said Kaush Amin, head of private market investing at US Bank Asset Management, adding that the current valuation "assumes years of rapid growth."

The debut has also done little to ease broader concerns about the health of the AI trade. Wall Street's main indexes ended sharply lower on Thursday, while futures pointed to further declines on Friday.

PARALLELS WITH SPACEX

Anthropic's IPO has drawn parallels with Elon Musk's SpaceX, whose June listing was the second-biggest on record.

Anthropic raised $93.5 billion in its IPO after underwriters exercised an option to buy additional shares, surpassing SpaceX's $85.7 billion haul to become the biggest listing on record.

While the companies have different business models, some investors have pointed to SpaceX's sharp swings in the weeks after its debut as a reason for caution over buying Anthropic immediately after its listing.

"There's going to be some volatility like we had with SpaceX. A lot of people are going to have FOMO. I don't think there's any need to get on it on the first trade," said Rob Hackel, CEO of financial advisory and brokerage firm RF Lafferty & Co.

SpaceX shares fell more than 6%.

Retail investors traded about $772 million of Anthropic shares on Thursday, the most for an IPO debut since Vanda Research began tracking the data in 2012.

The stock's sharp swings have left investors weighing the prospects of a rebound against further losses. Options trading, set to begin next week, could add to the volatility.

"It's not a good environment for Anthropic at the moment," said Carsten Hesse, head of index events at Berenberg.

(Reporting by Niket Nishant in Bengaluru; Additional reporting by Manya Saini, Anjana Jayakrishnan Nair and Echo Wang; Editing by Anil D'Silva and Vidya Ranganathan)

ATLANTA, Nov. 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- TIARA Talent Acquisition & Talent Tech Awards US has recognized Lendmark Financial Services (Lendmark) with the AgileOne Contingent Workforce Award, honoring the company's innovative and results-driven approach to workforce strategy and talent acquisition.

Selected from a field of leading employers, Lendmark earned top honors in a category that included finalists Danaher Corporation, Lyft and Transamerica.

The AgileOne Contingent Workforce Award recognizes organizations that demonstrate excellence in managing and developing contingent talent while delivering measurable business impact.

The strategy behind the award-winning program was created by Shalon Travis, Lendmark's senior vice president of talent acquisition and human resources systems, who led the development and execution of the winning workforce model. In recognizing Lendmark as the winner, the judges described the company's program as "a standout program that delivered impressive cost savings and measurable business impact through a strong contingent-to-permanent hiring strategy."

The judges also praised the company's integration of core LEND values into its talent strategy through its proprietary leadership model, which is built on Loyalty, Engaging, Nurturing and Decisiveness (LEND). "This award reflects who we are as a company and the values that guide how we support both our people and our customers," said Kelley Daviss, Chief Human Resources Officer for Lendmark. "Our contingent workforce program provides flexibility and cost savings while creating pathways for high-performing contingent workers to transition into full-time roles and continue their professional growth at Lendmark. We're proud to be recognized for an approach that delivers measurable business results while helping people build meaningful careers at Lendmark."

The TIARA Talent Acquisition & Talent Tech Awards, presented by TALiNT Partners, celebrate excellence, innovation and best practices in talent acquisition and workforce management across the United States. Winning organizations are selected through a rigorous judging process in which an independent panel of industry experts evaluates submissions based on innovation, measurable results and business impact, making the recognition a reflection of demonstrated organizational performance.

data.title: UK stocks sink as global selloff weighs on banks and miners
data.description:
(Updates to close)

Nov 20 - UK stocks fell on Friday, as a global selloff tied to worries about AI valuations and US interest rates dragged banking and mining stocks lower, overshadowing stronger-than-expected UK retail sales.

The blue-chip FTSE 100 index closed down 1.0% at 10,346.34 points, hitting a five-month low, while the mid-cap FTSE 250 index ended 2.2% lower at 23,651.73 after touching a four-month low.

* The selloff was part of a broader global market rout, with concern over AI-linked valuations and expectations for higher US interest rates pressuring risk assets

* The financial sector was the biggest drag on the index: HSBC ( HSBC ) dropped 3.6%, Standard Chartered ( SCBFF ) lost 5.6%, Barclays ( BCS ) fell 3.3% and NatWest Group ( NWG ) slipped 2.5%

* Precious and industrial metal miners were on course for a loss of more than 10% this week, dragged down by softer gold and copper prices, making them among FTSE's worst-performing sectors

* Shell dropped 1% and Ithaca Energy ( ITHLF ) dropped nearly 5% as oil prices fell, with Brent crude down about 1%, weighing on the sector

* Defensive consumer names offered some support. Unilever ( UL ) rose 2.2% to lead FTSE 100 gainers, while National Grid rose 1.1% and GSK added 0.8%

* On the data front, UK retail sales volumes unexpectedly rose 0.7% in October from September, bolstered by a government call for households to stock up on long-life items as well as stronger clothing sales

* Separately, UK government borrowing came in at £17 billion ($22.28 billion) in October, below forecasts of £18 billion, while earlier deficits were revised down by £3.6 billion, giving Chancellor John Healey some positive news on public finances

* Meanwhile, Britain and the European Union were set to deepen ties through agreements on easing food trade and youth mobility at a summit, and left open broader discussions about their long-term relationship

* The domestically-focused FTSE 250 logged its seventh straight day of declines, marking its longest losing streak since November 2025

* Decliners outnumbered advancers by a 5.7-to-1 margin in the London market

(Reporting by Darshan Kumar and Medha Singh in Bengaluru; Editing by Diti Pujara)

data.title: Anthropic's Tom Brown plans to donate to Trump's investment accounts for kids, source says

WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown will donate to US President Donald Trump's cradle-to-adulthood investment program known as Trump Accounts, according to a source familiar with the donation, joining a slew of wealthy individuals supporting the initiative.

Anthropic raised $93.5 billion in ​its blockbuster IPO on Thursday after underwriters exercised an option to buy additional ​shares.

Brown's donation is the latest sign of Anthropic's effort to improve relations with the Trump administration. The AI developer and its CEO, Dario Amodei, have at times clashed with Trump and senior administration officials over AI policy. In recent months, Brown, Anthropic's chief compute officer, has emerged as a key liaison to the administration, appearing at a technology-focused G20 event hosted by the US in August and at the September launch of a government AI tool.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in an interview with CNBC on Friday that an Anthropic founder would donate to the program "over the next few weeks," without naming Brown.

Trump Accounts provide government-funded investment accounts of $1,000 to US citizens born between 2025 and 2028. The program aims to promote investing and financial literacy from an early age.

(Reporting by Doina Chiacu and Courtney Rozen in Washington; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama )

data.title: Take-Two shatters sales record as 'GTA VI' launches to massive fanfare
data.description:
Nov 20 (Reuters) - Criminal duo Lucia and Jason's blitz through Vice City in "GTA VI" helped Take-Two Interactive, the publisher of the blockbuster game that is now a global cultural phenomenon, rake in nearly $4 billion in first-day sales.

Take-Two Interactive, the parent company of GTA developer Rockstar Games, is not a household name despite its portfolio of massive hits, including the "Red Dead Redemption" franchise and the "NBA 2K" basketball series.

The game also sold 32.5 million units in pre-release and garnered $3.79 billion in day-one retail sales, Rockstar Games said on Friday. That is nearly five times the roughly $800 million GTA V made on its first day in 2013. It was widely regarded as the best-selling videogame in the first 24 hours.

Analytics firm Sensor Tower estimated that the company sold 24.5 million copies of GTA VI and $2.36 billion in pre-order revenue.

Take-Two had stayed tight-lipped about GTA VI demand since it opened for pre-orders in June, limiting commentary to saying demand has been "unprecedented" or "far exceeding expectations."

"The title is so widely anticipated, consumers appear very, very excited, and all the press so far has been universally positive, but we still aren't ready to declare victory," CEO Strauss Zelnick said on Take-Two's earnings call earlier this month.

"We tend to avoid claiming success before it occurs," he had said.

GTA VI MARKETING BLITZ

Take-Two has shelled out an estimated $1 billion or more in production costs for GTA VI, making it one of the most expensive entertainment projects.

Sensor Tower estimates that the game's promotional trailer, GTA VI "Extended Look", on Netflix in August helped drive a sixfold jump in pre-orders.

In Miami, which Vice City is based on, the city's NBA team celebrated the release on Wednesday with a Vice City-themed match.

Over the weekend, the company is hosting "GTA VI: The Festival" - a music show with a star-studded line-up that includes Grammy-winning rapper Cardi B, hip hop record producer Metro Boomin and rapper Travis Scott.

WHAT NEXT FOR TAKE-TWO?

Investors have been waiting to hear from Take-Two about its plans for a PC launch of GTA VI and an online version rollout. The online, multiplayer component of a videogame is crucial in turning the title into a recurring revenue engine.

Some industry analysts are expecting the PC launch and online mode in 2027.

Brokerage TD Cowen named Take-Two one of its 'Best Ideas' for 2027, with its analyst Doug Creutz upbeat about the company's financial prospects when the game releases online.

"The potential ceiling for GTA VI's long-term recurrent consumer spending performance is very high... 'when' and 'how big' the next GTA Online will be is the most important question for the stock, more so than GTA VI unit sales."

(Reporting by Deborah Sophia in Bengaluru; Editing by Leroy Leo, Sherry Jacob-Phillips and Shinjini Ganguli)

data.title: Trump says he still backs Lutnick, urges Nvidia's Huang to apologize
data.description:
WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Friday he still supported Howard Lutnick, calling him "a very good businessman" as a scandal at AI chipmaker Nvidia raises questions about Lutnick's handling of Chinese chip sales.

Trump, speaking to reporters at a press conference following his trip to Asia this week, also said he discussed Nvidia's ( NVDA ) co-founder and now-former CEO Jensen Huang with Chinese President Xi Jinping but gave no other details about their conversation.

Reports that Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a company executive and ties to a suspected Chinese spy triggered his resignation and sparked investigations by US regulators and the FBI, congressional action, an internal review and a proposed investor class-action lawsuit.

US Senator Tom Cotton, an Arkansas Republican, told the Wall Street Journal earlier on Friday that Lutnick repeatedly ignored warnings that US artificial-intelligence chips were being smuggled to China before the Nvidia scandal became public but stopped short of saying he should resign.

Democrats, who take over Congress in January, meanwhile are probing whether Lutnick used his office to help investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald, which is controlled by his sons, avoid losses stemming from scrutiny of Nvidia's ( NVDA ) ties to a Chinese firm.

"I have not lost confidence. He's a different kind of a guy, very good businessman," Trump told reporters. "I think he's doing a very good job."

Trump also said he'd like to see the former Nvidia chief "make a big apology and go back," adding: "I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, 'Oh, brilliant, brilliant - he's a brilliant man.' He is."

His comments contradict those by his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who told CNBC in an interview earlier on Friday that the former Nvidia CEO did not come up in talks.

The New York Times reported on Friday that the suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, has extensive ties to China's defense industry.

Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the US Senate in a public hearing, an aide to the Senate Banking chairman said on Friday, though a representative for Huang declined to comment. Huang is also scheduled to speak to US House lawmakers behind closed doors in early December.

(Reporting by Bo Erickson in Washington; additional reporting by Katharine Jackson and Susan Heavey in Washington and Rodrigo Ramirez in Mexico City; Editing by Sanjeev Miglani)

By Stephen Culp and Utkarsh Hathi

NEW YORK, Nov 20 (Reuters) - US stocks extended their rout on Friday, putting the S&P 500 and the Dow on course to confirm corrections after Anthropic's momentous debut fell flat, exacerbating worries over the AI trade that has driven this year's stock market rally.

All three major US equity indexes were sharply lower, with the Dow and the S&P 500 now more than 10% below their record closing highs reached on October 6. Should those levels hold, it would confirm both indexes entered corrections on that date.

The bellwether S&P 500 is poised to notch its seventh consecutive drop, which would mark its longest losing streak since February 2020.

All three indexes are on track to log their largest weekly percentage losses since April 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced his market-rattling "liberation day" tariff package.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq entered negative territory for the year.

data.title: Exclusive-Nvidia's accounting is a focus of US SEC investigation, sources say
data.description:
NEW YORK/WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The US Securities and Exchange Commission is probing Nvidia's accounting practices, said two people briefed on the matter, adding to the legal woes facing the scandal-hit chip giant.

The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday reported that the SEC was probing Nvidia but said it could not ascertain the focus of the investigation. The people, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential issues, said SEC enforcement staff are scrutinizing potential accounting issues at the company.

A spokesperson for the SEC declined to comment. Spokespeople for Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Reuters could not immediately determine when the SEC opened its inquiry or exactly what potential accounting issues the watchdog is examining. Investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and many close without resulting in enforcement action.

Still, the accounting focus of the probe, which Reuters is reporting for the first time, increases pressure on Nvidia, whose investors are still reeling from revelations about ousted CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital relationships, including with Alice Huang, who US authorities suspect is a Chinese spy. China has denied she is a spy.

Alice Huang led Singapore-based Megaspeed, historically a large Nvidia chip customer, people familiar with the matter have said. US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over possible violations of export controls related to alleged shipments of Nvidia AI chips to China, the US Justice and Commerce departments said this week.

The crisis has sent shares in Nvidia, a linchpin of the AI boom, tumbling more than a third and stoked calls in Washington for tougher action on tech threats posed by Beijing.

Megaspeed has said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and that it conducted "lawful business." Reuters has not been able to reach Alice Huang. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair in a November 8 statement following the reports of his relationship with Alice Huang, without referring to her by name.

The SEC probe is the latest of Nvidia's legal woes. The Justice Department has also been reviewing Nvidia's $12.9-billion deal to buy open-source platform Hugging Face alongside a broader antitrust investigation into the company's acquisitions and practices, Reuters reported last month.

SINGAPORE ACCOUNTING CHANGE BACK IN FOCUS

Last year, Nvidia changed how it reports geographic revenue, using customer headquarters rather than billing addresses, which it said would better reflect the geographic profile of its revenue. The change resulted in Singapore being removed from its geographical breakdown.

The Financial Times, citing company accounts, reported on Tuesday that Nvidia had made the change even as Singapore sales soared to almost half its global revenue.

That accounting shift has drawn renewed press scrutiny in the wake of the Alice Huang scandal.

Southeast Asia has become a hub for chip smuggling to China since the Biden administration barred advanced AI chip exports to that country over concerns they could boost Beijing's military.

Analysts and investors have also grown increasingly concerned about circular AI financing deals, in which chipmakers including Nvidia have pursued complex financial arrangements to help customers fund purchases of their chips and the construction of costly AI infrastructure, such as data centers. Nvidia has backed AI companies and cloud providers and provided guarantees connected to data-center projects that use its equipment.

Critics say such arrangements can make it harder for investors to assess the quality of chipmakers' revenue and their true financial exposure. Speaking to Reuters last month, SEC enforcement chief David Woodcock said the agency was examining AI companies' corporate disclosures to ensure issuers are giving investors the full picture on potential risks.

On its Tuesday earnings call, Nvidia's interim CEO and former CFO Colette Kress said the company was proud of its role in supporting the AI industry, but would be far more selective moving forward about AI industry financing deals.

The SEC under President Donald Trump has pulled back on enforcement, saying it will focus on bread-and-butter securities fraud, including accounting violations that have long been a mainstay of its enforcement work. It recently launched a new financial reporting and accounting unit within its enforcement division, aimed at developing cases in accounting and auditing areas.

(Reporting by Chris Prentice in New York and Alexandra Alper in Washington; Additional reporting by Karen Freifeld and Jody Godoy in New York; Editing by Michelle Price and Daniel Wallis)

data.title: Trump says US to penalize firms building data centers abroad
data.description:
WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Friday that the US would penalize American companies that build data centers overseas, a move he said is intended to help the US artificial intelligence sector compete with its Chinese counterparts. 

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country," Trump said while discussing AI at a White House news conference following his trip to Asia. He said he would impose a "tremendous tax" on companies that build data centers abroad.

Data centers are critical to the AI boom because they provide the computing power needed to train and run increasingly complex AI systems, and a penalty could complicate the global AI buildout. Several major American data center developers build and operate such facilities outside the US, including Equinix ( EQIX ) and Digital Realty. 

Data center developers often locate facilities close to users to reduce delays for time-sensitive tasks such as payment processing. Transmitting large volumes of data over long distances can also add significant costs.

Trump has been a staunch advocate for data center construction in the US, a position that is unpopular with voters. Data centers have drawn opposition in communities nationwide over concerns about electricity demand, utility costs and other local impacts.

The Commerce Department moved on Monday to restrict exports of advanced AI chips to several Southeast Asian countries, part of a broader effort to prevent China from obtaining the technology through third countries.

 The United States already bars direct sales of the most advanced AI chips to China, but Chinese companies have continued to access them by renting computing capacity at data centers in countries that can legally import the chips.

(Reporting by Bo Erickson and Katharine Jackson; Writing by Doina Chiacu; Editing by Caitlin Webber and Sanjeev Miglani)

Diabetes care is moving out of the clinic and onto the wrist, the arm and the smartphone. Continuous glucose monitors (CGM), automated insulin delivery (AID) systems, smart insulin pens and cloud platforms now feed data to patients and care teams in near real time. The International Diabetes Federation estimates that 589 million adults were living with diabetes in 2024, a figure projected to reach 853 million by 2050, which gives the sector a large and growing patient base. Care Is Shifting From the Clinic to the Home

Glooko's 2025 Global Diabetes Report found that remote diabetes data uploads overtook in-clinic uploads in early 2024, and by the end of that year remote uploads were about 1.5 times higher. The analysis tracked device synchronization across North America and EMEA between June 2020 and June 2025. For healthcare providers, connected platforms mean glucose patterns and time-in-range can be reviewed between appointments, so treatment can be adjusted without waiting for the next visit.

Type 2 Diabetes Is the Next Big Growth Pool

CGM and AID were built around Type 1 diabetes, but manufacturers are now extending them to broader groups. In August 2024, the U.S. FDA expanded the indication for Insulet's SmartAdjust technology to adults with Type 2 diabetes. A 2025 randomized trial of 72 adults with Type 2 diabetes not taking insulin found that CGM users raised time-in-range from 46% to 72% over six months, with a 1.3-percentage-point reduction in HbA1c. Results from small trials need confirming in larger studies, but they help explain why companies are targeting this population.

Over-the-counter products are widening access further:

  • Automated Insulin Delivery: Systems that connect sensors, pumps and dosing algorithms reduce manual insulin calculations and the daily burden of treatment.
  • Broader User Base: Connected devices are becoming relevant for insulin-treated Type 2 diabetes, not only Type 1.
  • Reimbursement: Insurers and public programs are extending coverage for monitoring devices, which improves affordability.
  • Remote Monitoring and Integration: Linking CGM data with smartphones, electronic health records and connected insulin devices consolidates fragmented patient information.

Challenges Facing the Digital Diabetes Management Market

Cost is the biggest barrier. Sensors, pumps and consumables carry recurring costs, and in the U.S., Medicare CGM coverage remains tied to insulin treatment or documented problematic hypoglycemia. A 2025 study across six low- and middle-income countries found sensor prices of roughly USD 88 to 107 each, and a month's supply required about 15 to 65 days of wages. Other hurdles include interoperability between manufacturers, data privacy and cybersecurity, patchy connectivity and limited digital health literacy.

In November 2026, Tandem Diabetes Care, Inc. of the United States received multiple Health Canada approvals for its t:slim X2 insulin pump with Control-IQ+ technology. In January 2026, Medtronic received FDA clearance for MiniMed Go, which pairs its InPen smart insulin pen with the Instinct sensor for people on multiple daily injections.

data.title: Taiwan's Stock Pickers Are Walking Out to Bet Their Own Money
data.description:
NEW YORK, Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Fly On Wall Street News Commentary - Taiwan's benchmark stock index was up 62% this year, the best showing of any major equity gauge in the world, when Bloomberg reported on Oct. 16 that some of the island's professional fund managers and analysts are quitting their jobs to invest their own money. Strict rules keep them from trading the very stocks they pick for clients, and in a year when about one in ten stocks in the index has more than doubled, some have decided the trade-off is no longer worth it. Companies and funds mentioned in this article include: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited ( TSM ) [TSMC] , ASE Technology Holding Co., Ltd. ( ASX ) [ASE] , United Microelectronics Corporation ( UMC ) [UMC] , iShares MSCI Taiwan ETF , The Taiwan Fund, Inc. ( TWN ) .

Watching From Behind the Locker

Taiwan does not ban personal investing outright, but its asset-management code of conduct bars staff from trading a locally listed stock or a linked derivative within seven business days before or after their firm's funds trade it, which in practice rules out personal stock-picking. Fund managers must also lock away their phones, laptops and smartwatches each morning until the market closes at 1:30 p.m. The phone rule was formalized in 2024 to deter insider trading, the Taipei Times reported in July, after six former fund managers from four firms were indicted for front-running trades through the accounts of relatives and friends.

Ken Tsai, 40, a fund manager who until July worked at a large Taiwanese asset manager that Bloomberg did not name, told Bloomberg he made a Taiwanese maker of AI-server data-transfer components his fund's largest holding in 2024. The stock rose more than fivefold in 2025 and about sixfold again this year, but he owned none of it personally. "It left me with a strong sense of relative deprivation," he said. He now works at a private investment firm in Taipei, which was also not named. Pay adds to the pull: Taiwan portfolio managers earn roughly US$124,000 to US$311,000 a year, well below Hong Kong base salaries, according to Bloomberg, citing headhunters and recruitment-firm data.

The private shops they are joining sit outside those rules. They register as private companies with the Ministry of Economic Affairs and do not need asset-management licenses from the Financial Supervisory Commission because they do not raise public money. Brokers told Bloomberg some of them now generate more than NT$10 billion in monthly trading volume, rivaling mid-sized asset managers.

The Rally Behind the Exits

Much of the rally traces back to the AI hardware supply chain. TSMC reported third-quarter revenue of NT$1.49 trillion (US$46.7 billion) on Oct. 15, up 50.9% from a year earlier, while net income jumped 68.7% and gross margin reached 66.4%. It guided fourth-quarter revenue from US$52.3 billion to US$54.3 billion.

Chip packaging and testing has ridden the same wave. ASE Technology ( ASX ) reported September net revenue of NT$88.1 billion, up 45.5% from a year earlier, and third-quarter revenue of NT$244.2 billion, up 44.8%.

Mature-node foundry UMC reported August sales up 30.71% from a year earlier, lifting year-to-date sales 14.66%. In its second-quarter report, the company guided for capacity utilization above 90% in the third quarter and said revenue from its 22/28nm business continues to set record highs.

CONTINUED... Read more market coverage at: flyonwallstreet.com

A Talent Squeeze, Not a Stampede

The numbers point to churn more than an exodus. Fewer than half of Taiwan's 20 largest local equity mutual funds have kept the same portfolio manager for more than three years, according to fund-data site MoneyDJ, and Bloomberg reported that applications for junior roles at some international firms have roughly halved this year. Yet the FSC said the industry's registered headcount actually rose to 4,729 in September from 4,581 at the end of 2025. Firms are responding: the largest foreign asset manager in Taiwan is offering cross-market analyst roles and office rotations to keep staff.

Regulators are paying attention. The FSC said on Oct. 15 it is gathering information and plans to review the rules, balancing market development against conflicts of interest and investor protection. One asset-management executive told Bloomberg there is no easy solution for now.

The Case for the Pros

At least one professionally managed fund has kept pace. The Taiwan Fund ( TWN ), a closed-end fund listed in New York, reported a 47.36% total return for its fiscal quarter ended May 31, against 26.12% for the TAIEX Total Return Index over the same period, with net asset value of US$116.90 a share at the end of that quarter.

Investors who prefer to own the whole market can use the iShares MSCI Taiwan ETF, which holds about US$11.9 billion in assets.

Last week was a reminder of how quickly the math can change. The TAIEX fell 4.6%, its first weekly decline in five weeks, as a technology selloff spread and TSMC CEO C.C. Wei warned of macroeconomic uncertainty and weak consumer demand, according to Trading Economics. In New York, TSMC's shares fell 8.98% from the Oct. 9 close to $412.61 on Oct. 16, ASE dropped 14.86% to $39.53, UMC slid 13.68% to $19.82, the iShares fund lost 7.04% to $106.26 and The Taiwan Fund ( TWN ) declined 8.78% to $94.18, according to Stock Analysis data. For the managers who just traded a salary for their own account, those swings now land on them.

data.title: FCC grants tech import waivers as firms boost US investment
data.description:
WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The Federal Communications Commission said on Friday it has granted approvals to 71 companies in 2026 to continue importing drones, wireless routers, robots and power inverters that would have been barred under US national security restrictions.

The US telecommunications regulator is trying to push Chinese gear out of ​technology supply chains and spur domestic manufacturing.

The FCC said the companies that have won approvals have agreed to invest $4.4 billion and create 4,700 jobs to move tech equipment production as a condition of approval for the waivers. The so-called Covered List has been used by the FCC to ban tech equipment on national security grounds and has been one of the most significant parts of the Trump administration's China policy.

"The FCC's Covered List has proven to be an essential tool in our national security toolkit, protecting America's networks and communications infrastructure from dangerous products," said FCC Chair Brendan Carr, a Republican, adding that it has "also generated a surge in investment in American manufacturing."

The Covered List has been used by the FCC to ban new Chinese drones, robots, routers and power inverters. Reuters has reported that the FCC could use ‌the list ⁠to ban imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers that are crucial to data centers.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, a Democrat, on Thursday questioned how the list has been used.

"Its original purpose was to keep insecure equipment out of our networks, and that is targeted towards adversary countries," Gomez said. She added that the Trump administration has used the Covered List for items with ties to telecom or IT equipment "to gain concessions that have nothing to do with security" and that it has "instead become an industrial policy tool."

In September, the Republican chair of the US House of Representatives Energy and Commerce Committee and the panel's top Democrat proposed overhauling use of the Covered List.

The proposed legislation signaled congressional concern about how the FCC is ⁠using its authority to restrict Chinese technology and would require the agency to seek input from other government agencies ​before determining whether foreign technology poses an unacceptable national security risk.

(Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Paul Simao)

data.title: Trump says US to penalize firms building data centers abroad
data.description:
WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Friday that the US would penalize American companies that build data centers overseas, a move he said is intended to help the US artificial intelligence sector compete with its Chinese counterparts. 

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country," Trump said while discussing AI at a White House news conference following his trip to Asia. He said he would impose a "tremendous tax" on companies that build data centers abroad.

Data centers are critical to the AI boom because they provide the computing power needed to train and run increasingly complex AI systems, and a penalty could complicate the global AI buildout. Several major American data center developers build and operate such facilities outside the US, including Equinix ( EQIX ) and Digital Realty. 

Data center developers often locate facilities close to users to reduce delays for time-sensitive tasks such as payment processing. Transmitting large volumes of data over long distances can also add significant costs.

Trump has been a staunch advocate for data center construction in the US, a position that is unpopular with voters. Data centers have drawn opposition in communities nationwide over concerns about electricity demand, utility costs and other local impacts.

The Commerce Department moved on Monday to restrict exports of advanced AI chips to several Southeast Asian countries, part of a broader effort to prevent China from obtaining the technology through third countries.

 The United States already bars direct sales of the most advanced AI chips to China, but Chinese companies have continued to access them by renting computing capacity at data centers in countries that can legally import the chips.

(Reporting by Bo Erickson and Katharine Jackson; Writing by Doina Chiacu; Editing by Caitlin Webber and Sanjeev Miglani)

data.title: Trump says only older chips should be sold to China

"We want only older chips, and we don't mind if none go. But only older. You have to understand, China makes chips too, and if we're not going to sell them, they'll make them themselves," he told reporters at a press conference following his trip to Asia.

Those remarks followed an earlier answer to a question about whether he was considering easing up export bans on chips to China after meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, to which Trump responded: "We're talking about a very comprehensive deal with China."

Trump's administration on Monday, ahead of the trip, said it would further restrict China's access to advanced AI chips from companies like Nvidia ( NVDA ).

data.title: China's BYD has SUV that infringes on JLR Defender design, Dutch court rules
data.description:
LONDON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - A judge at the Dutch district court in The Hague ruled on Friday that a large SUV made by BYD infringes on the design of Jaguar Land Rover's popular Defender model and imposed a temporary injunction prohibiting the Chinese automaker from selling the vehicle in the European Union.

JLR, a unit of India's Tata Motors, launched the case earlier this year after BYD announced on its UK web site that the seven-seater Ti7 SUV was available for orders with deliveries to customers starting in January 2027.

BYD launched the Fangchengbao Ti7 in China last year.

"In these summary proceedings, the preliminary relief judge rules that the Ti7 infringes the EU design of Jaguar Land Rover," the court ruling said. "The characteristic and distinctive elements of the design are reflected in the BYD Ti7."

The temporary injunction is for a week because the court found that BYD "currently has no concrete plans to place the Ti7 on the market in the EU."

The judge ruled, however, that the court had no jurisdiction over BYD's affiliate in the United Kingdom.

It is rare in Europe for major automakers to go to court over design rights infringement. It is also uncommon for such a ruling to come so early in proceedings of a case that is ongoing and likely to last for some time.

"We protect our intellectual property and take legal action when necessary," JLR said in a statement. "Legal proceedings are ongoing, and we won't be commenting further at this time."

Legacy automakers have often complained that Chinese automakers have copied designs, though little has been proven in court. In 2005, for instance, General Motors ( GM ) and Chinese rival Chery settled a case over the Chery QQ that the No. 1 US automaker said was a copy of its Chevrolet Spark.

In a statement, BYD said it "strongly disagrees" with the ruling and will appeal it.

"The BYD Ti 7 is the result of BYD's own independent design work and infringes none of JLR's rights," BYD said. "We will pursue every legal avenue to demonstrate that this decision is incorrect."

BYD has grown rapidly in Europe since launching sales on the continent in late 2022. According to ACEA data, this year through September the Chinese automaker's sales more than doubled to over 280,000 vehicles in Europe versus the same period last year, outselling Ford, Tesla and Nissan.

(Reporting By Nick Carey; Editing by Toby Chopra)
